title: How to choose qualitative coding software: a buyer’s guide for research teams
summary: Learn the three types of qualitative coding software, what to check before you buy, and when to move beyond traditional CAQDAS. Plus, 10 popular tools compared.
body_markdown:
If we standardize on one qualitative coding tool, how do we make sure codes and themes stay comparable across studies and researchers? +


Start with one shared codebook that every researcher works from, with a short definition for each code so it’s applied the same way each time. Add a review step where a second researcher checks a sample of coded passages and flags disagreements before findings are final. Then keep every study in one place, so a code applied to this quarter’s focus group transcripts means the same thing in next year’s follow-up. Without these, teams rebuild the codebook for each project, and themes can’t be tracked from one study to the next.


What should I ask a qualitative coding software vendor about audit trails, permissions, and who changed a codebook? +


Ask whether the software logs every change to a code or the codebook, with who made it and when. Ask whether you can limit who edits the codebook separately from who can view or apply codes, and whether you can export the change log for a compliance review. Also check which plan includes these controls, since some vendors keep advanced features like role-based permissions for their higher-priced packages. A clear change log lets you show how a finding was reached if someone questions it.


How do licensing and seat models typically work for qualitative coding software when usage spreads beyond the original project team? +


A lot of qualitative coding software is priced per user, per project or through a company-wide contract. Desktop QDA tools have traditionally sold per-user licenses that you download and install on each device, often with discounted university pricing. Browser-based tools usually charge per seat each month. Per-user pricing gets expensive as research spreads, since every new stakeholder needs an extra license. Ask vendors about volume discounts, annual contracts and view-only access for people who only need to read findings. Free tools and open source software options cover basic functionality without license costs, but they rarely include the SSO, admin controls and support an enterprise rollout needs.


Can we migrate our existing projects, codebooks, and memos from our current tool without breaking longitudinal comparisons? +


Usually, but check the details first. Ask vendors which file formats they import, whether codes, memos and coded passages come across intact, and how they handle data types beyond text, such as survey data, audio, video and images. Ask whether they support REFI-QDA, an open standard for moving coded projects between QDA tools. Raw research materials like Word documents and transcripts usually move easily. The coding on top of them is what tends to break, so migrate one past study as a test and check that its codes still line up with your current codebook before moving the rest. If you’re moving to Conveo, it can analyze interview recordings you’ve already collected, so earlier interviews aren’t left behind.


Is there free qualitative coding software? +


Yes. QualCoder and Taguette are free, open-source tools. QualCoder supports multimedia data and runs on multiple operating systems, while Taguette is a web-based platform with basic coding functionality. RQDA is a plugin for the R programming language, but it hasn’t been maintained since 2021. Free qualitative data coding software suits students and small projects, but it doesn’t list security certifications or offer SSO, which most enterprise IT teams require.


How long does it take to learn qualitative coding software? +


The learning curve for qualitative coding software varies among different platforms. Delve allows immediate coding without installation hassles. Feature-heavy desktop tools like NVivo qualitative coding software and ATLAS.ti are built for complex projects and can take days of training. Ask vendors what training and support they offer before you commit.
